extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of elementary/Euclidean geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Study and application of theorems, problems, and definitions from Book II (theory of rectangles, algebraic identities, constructions like extreme-and-mean ratio) and the opening of Book III (theory of the circle) of a geometry textbook based on Euclid. Includes propositions, constructions, corollaries and exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation: square on sum minus square on difference equals four times rectangle
rubrics_metrics.description: For any two lines, four times the rectangle contained by them is equal to the square on their sum minus the square on their difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived directly from previously established identities: square on sum = sum of squares + twice the rectangle; square on difference = sum of squares − twice the rectangle; subtracting yields 4×rectangle. Appears as algebraic-geometric identity used repeatedly in constructions and proofs in Book II.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. IX — sum of squares on unequal parts when a line is bisected
rubrics_metrics.description: If line AB is bisected at C and divided into two unequal parts at D, then the sum of the squares on AD and DB equals twice the sum of the squares on AC and on CD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric construction using perpendicular CE equal to AC, parallels and right-triangle square relations. Also shown algebraically: AD = AC + CD, DB = AC − CD; squaring and adding yields AD^2 + DB^2 = 2 AC^2 + 2 CD^2. Exercises follow (minimization, loci, related triangle and parallelogram identities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. X — sum of squares when line is bisected and divided externally
rubrics_metrics.description: If line AB is bisected at C and divided externally at D, then the sum of the squares on AD and DB equals twice the square on half the line plus twice the square on the segment between the points of section (i.e., AD^2 + BD^2 = 2 AC^2 + 2 CD^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction mirrors Prop. IX with external division; proofs use right triangles and equalities of corresponding segments. Algebraic form: AD = CD + AC, BD = CD − AC; squaring and adding gives stated identity. Exercises and corollaries provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enunciations summarising Book II identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Three compact algebraic-geometric identities: (1) square on sum + square on difference = twice the sum of their squares; (2) sum of the squares on two lines = twice the square on half their sum + twice the square on half their difference; (3) comparison of sums of squares for equal vs unequal partitions and the relation by the squares of the differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are presented as consequences/corollaries of earlier propositions (IV, VII, etc.) and used as tools in many constructions and problem solutions throughout Book II. Exercises ask to apply them to solve for lines from given sums/differences and to derive loci.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XI — problem: divide a line so AB·BH = square on other segment (extreme and mean ratio)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct point H on AB so that rectangle AB·BH equals the square on AH. The construction produces the division in 'extreme and mean ratio' (the golden-section construction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: describe square on AB, bisect diagonal, extend and construct a square on extension; deduce equality of certain rectangles and squares to show AB·BH = AH^2. Corollaries: properties of repeated division, inequalities (greater/less segments), and proof that parts of such a division are incommensurable. Exercises: cut a line externally in extreme & mean ratio; algebraic relations among squares on segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — 'extreme and mean ratio' (golden section)
rubrics_metrics.description: A line divided so that the rectangle (whole × one segment) equals the square on the other segment is said to be divided in 'extreme and mean ratio'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollaries describe iterative properties (how the greater segment is cut similarly by taking a part equal to the lesser, etc.) and the consequence that parts so divided are incommensurable. Exercises explore numeric identities and triangle constructions involving this ratio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XII — obtuse-triangle analogue of Pythagoras (law-of-cosines form)
rubrics_metrics.description: In an obtuse-angled triangle ABC (obtuse at C), the square on the side AB (subtending the obtuse angle) exceeds the sum of the squares on BC and CA by twice the rectangle contained by either of them (BC) and its continuation CD to meet the perpendicular AD from the opposite angle: AB^2 = BC^2 + CA^2 + 2·BC·CD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof given by splitting BD and using prior square-sum identities; an alternative proof via squares on sides and perpendicular constructions is sketched. Corollaries and exercises apply this to perpendiculars from vertices and special ratio cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XIII — acute-triangle analogue of Pythagoras (law-of-cosines form)
rubrics_metrics.description: In an acute-angled triangle ABC (acute at C), the square on side AB is less than the sum of the squares on AC and BC by twice the rectangle of BC and the intercept CD between the acute angle and the foot of the perpendicular from the opposite angle: AB^2 = AC^2 + BC^2 − 2·BC·CD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by adding square identities for segments created by the foot of perpendicular; alternative demonstration via squares-on-sides construction is provided. Exercises explore specialized angle values and related quadrilateral/median identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XIV — problem: construct a square equal to a given rectilineal figure
rubrics_metrics.description: Given any rectilineal figure X (converted to a rectangle AC equal to X), construct a square of equal area by transforming adjacent unequal sides into equal ones via extending a side, bisecting the extension, and using a semicircle construction to find a segment BG whose square equals AC (hence X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction uses the standard semicircle/square method: extend AB to E making BE = BC, bisect AE at F, describe semicircle with FE radius, meet extension of CB at G; BG^2 = AC. Corollary: square on perpendicular from a point in a semicircle equals rectangle contained by diameter segments. Exercises: invert related problems (given differences/rectangles find lines) and applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collection of Exercises and Examination Questions for Book II
rubrics_metrics.description: A long list of exercises and exam questions testing understanding of Book II: theory of rectangles, extremal properties (max/min of products and sums of squares), constructions (extracting square roots, dividing lines), loci (circles from given sums of squares), incommensurability, and numerical problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions include both geometric constructions and algebraic verifications; they are explicitly posed after propositions and intended for student practice and examination. They indicate the expected competency and typical problem types for Book II.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book III — Definitions of circle theory (i–xvi)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions covering fundamental circle concepts: equal circles (equal radii), chord and secant, tangent (touch), kinds of contact between circles, segment and arc (major/minor), chord-distance from centre, angle in a segment, angle of a segment (between chord and tangent), sector, concentric circles, concyclic points, cyclic quadrilateral, expanded notion of angle (rotation, positive/negative), ray.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions often include modern comments (Newcomb) and observations about modernized meanings (e.g., tangent defined as limit of secant). Several tacit theorems underlying definitions are noted; these definitions set vocabulary and expectations used in all subsequent Book III propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. I (Book III) — problem: find centre of a given circle
rubrics_metrics.description: Construction: take two distinct points on the circumference, bisect the chord between them, erect perpendicular; do likewise for another chord; intersection gives centre. Proof: perpendicular bisectors of chords meet at the centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollaries: any line bisecting a chord passes through centre; locus of centres of circles through two fixed points is the perpendicular bisector; three such perpendicular bisectors meet in centre. Exercise-level expectation: ability to carry out perpendicular-bisector construction and justify uniqueness of centre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. II (Book III) — segment between two points of circumference lies inside circle
rubrics_metrics.description: If two points A and B on a circle are connected by a straight segment, the segment between them lies inside the circle, while the extensions beyond A and B are outside the circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses triangle inequalities and radii comparisons. Corollaries: three collinear points cannot be concyclic; a line meets a circle in at most two points; circumference is concave towards the centre. This proposition sets geometric intuition about chords and secants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. III (Book III) — perpendicular bisector and centre relation for chords
rubrics_metrics.description: 1) A line through the centre that bisects a chord (which does not pass through the centre) cuts it at right angles. 2) Conversely, a line through the centre cutting a chord at right angles bisects it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof compares triangles formed by radii to chord endpoints and uses congruence. Corollaries: perpendicular bisector of a chord passes through centre, locus of midpoints of parallel chord system is the diameter perpendicular to them. Exercises apply to concentric circles and equal intercepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. IV (Book III) — two chords not both diameters cannot bisect each other
rubrics_metrics.description: Two chords of a circle which are not both diameters cannot bisect each other; if two chords bisect each other they must both be diameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction using the fact that perpendicular bisector through centre cannot produce a 'part equal to the whole'. This is used to characterize diameters among chords.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. V (Book III) — intersecting circles are not concentric
rubrics_metrics.description: If two circles cut one another at a point, they cannot have the same centre (i.e., non-concentric).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: assuming same centre leads to equality-of-radii contradictions. Exercise: show two non-concentric circles intersect in two points; no three common points unless coincident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. VI (Book III) — internal tangency prohibits common centre
rubrics_metrics.description: If one circle touches another internally at a point A, they are not concentric (cannot share the same centre).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate from Prop. V type reasoning; drawing another radius and comparing gives contradiction if centres coincide. This proposition clarifies possible configurations of tangent circles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. VII (Book III) — extrema and ordering of chords from interior point
rubrics_metrics.description: From a point P inside a circle (but not the centre), the greatest line to the circumference is the one passing through the centre; its opposite production is the least. Among others, those nearer the diameter through P are longer than more remote ones. Equal angles on opposite sides yield equal chord lengths; more than two equal radii from P to circumference is impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple-part result proved via triangle inequalities, comparisons of angles and sides. Corollaries: diameter through P bisects angle between two equal lines from P; concentric-circle-radius relations (max/min and touching relations) follow. Exercises: use as definition of maxima/minima in geometrical variation contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. VIII (Book III) — extrema and ordering of chords from exterior point
rubrics_metrics.description: From a point P outside a circle: to the concave (inner) circumference the longest line is that through the centre, with nearer lines longer than more remote; to the convex circumference the minimum occurs when produced through the centre, with nearer-to-minimum lines smaller than more remote ones. Equal lines can be drawn in pairs making equal angles with the line through the centre; more than two equal such lines cannot be drawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs mirror Prop. VII but use external triangle inequalities and angle comparisons. Corollaries: equality of certain intercepted segments when lines are extended, bisecting properties of diameters, and constraints on number of equal segments from an external point.
